proposals.explanation: BitBox support documentation states the BitBoxApp does not embed third-party tracking, advertising, or analytics tools.
The BitBoxApp does not embed third-party tracking/analytics/crash tools; logging is anonymized and minimized, with no third-party crash reporting described.
No stealth-address receiving is offered; the BitBoxApp supports standard Bitcoin and basic Ethereum/ERC20 receiving only.
No Privacy Pools integration is documented in the BitBoxApp changelog or support materials.
All transfers are ordinary on-chain public transactions with no private/shielded mode offered in the BitBoxApp send flow.
The BitBoxApp offers WalletConnect dapp connectivity but no built-in token-approval inspection/revocation UI; users are directed to external tools like Etherscan for approvals.
The BitBoxApp can connect to the user's own Bitcoin full node via an Electrum-compatible server for independent verification and broadcast.
No native cross-chain bridging is documented in the BitBoxApp changelog or support hub.
BitBox publishes a public CHANGELOG.md for the BitBoxApp and a separate firmware changelog on GitHub.
BitBoxApp installers are code-signed/notarized with published GPG .asc signatures, and firmware releases carry signed reproducibility assertions.
BitBox02 firmware is built reproducibly via Docker with fixed dependencies, allowing anyone to rebuild and match the official binary from a version tag.
The cySync-desktop README lists 'Disable analytics' only for development mode, indicating analytics telemetry is enabled in production builds.
The cySync-desktop README lists 'Disable crash report' only for development mode, indicating crash reporting is active in production builds.
No Cypherock documentation or feature page references stealth-address receiving, which is absent from this hardware wallet and its cySync app.
No Cypherock source mentions Privacy Pools integration in the X1 or cySync app.
As a standard multi-chain hardware wallet with no privacy-transfer mode, token transfers are public by default.
Cypherock states swapping and bridging functionalities related to cross-chain bridging are not available; only swaps are offered, not native bridging.
cySync provides portfolio aggregation tracking assets across wallets and chains in a single place, giving a unified account value view.
Cypherock publishes detailed public firmware release notes with version numbers and changes on its GitHub releases page.
WalletScrutiny confirms X1 firmware is signed by two private keys with a signed header appended to the firmware binary image.
Firefly is an air-gapped DIY hardware wallet with no wireless/wired data connection, so the device cannot send usage telemetry per firefly.city.
The device is air-gapped and cannot transmit signals, and neither the firmware nor docs mention any crash/error reporting.
No stealth-address support is mentioned anywhere in the Firefly firmware, hardware docs, or firefly.city site.
No Privacy Pools integration is referenced in the Firefly firmware or any official material.
Firefly signs standard public Ethereum transactions with no private-transfer mode described.
Firefly is an Ethereum-only signing device with no built-in cross-chain bridging described in any official source.
Being an air-gapped single-chain Ethereum signer with no balance-aggregating companion suite, there is no unified cross-chain balance view.
Firefly's companion Ethers Wallet uses ethers.js which resolves ENS names (e.g. ricmoo.firefly.eth), and ENS destination resolution is an explicit Firefly design goal.
The Firefly Pixie hardware repo publishes a public CHANGELOG.md tracking changes between board revisions.
The Firefly Pixie firmware README states BSD License while the hardware design repo is MIT License.
GridPlus documentation states it does not collect user data on the Lattice Manager and end-to-end encrypts device messages, with no usage telemetry indicated.
No GridPlus documentation or repo indicates support for stealth-address receiving on the Lattice1 or its companion apps.
No GridPlus documentation or integration lists Privacy Pools support.
The Lattice1 signs standard on-chain Bitcoin and Ethereum transactions with no privacy transfer mode, so transfers are public by default.
The official Lattice Manager only handles device management and simple BTC send/receive, with no token-approval inspection or revocation feature documented.
GridPlus offers lattice-connect-v2, a self-hosted endpoint users run on their own network to sign and route transactions without any GridPlus infrastructure.
Neither the Lattice1 firmware nor the Lattice Manager provides native cross-chain bridging functionality.
The Lattice Manager offers a simple BTC wallet and device management but no unified cross-chain account value view.
GridPlus publishes a public changelog of firmware/software releases in the lattice-software-releases GitHub repo and firmware release blog posts.
GridPlus firmware documentation states every release must be signed by multiple geographically separated private keys and verified by a secure bootloader before installation.
The Lattice1 firmware is proprietary/closed-source while GridPlus's supporting tools like gridplus-sdk and eth-lattice-keyring are MIT and the lattice-manager repo specifies no license.
imToken (imKey Pro's primary companion app) uses Firebase for usage statistics/analytics per its security documentation.
imToken uses Sentry for error/crash reporting per its official security documentation.
No imKey or imToken documentation indicates support for stealth-address receiving; it is not a listed feature.
Neither imKey nor its companion imToken app documents any Privacy Pools integration.
imKey Pro signs standard public on-chain transactions (BTC, ETH/ERC-20, TRX) with no private-transfer mode.
imToken supports custom network RPC configuration, available for imKey and imKey Pro, allowing broadcast via a self-hosted node endpoint.
imToken supports ENS registration, management, and forward/reverse .eth resolution per its help center.
The imToken companion app publishes public per-version release notes on the App Store.
WalletScrutiny states imKey Pro builds cannot be reproduced because the current-release source code is not publicly available.
Keycard Shell is an air-gapped QR transaction signer whose official docs, blog and firmware repo describe only BTC/ETH/ERC-20/ERC-712 clear signing with no mention of stealth-address receiving.
No Privacy Pools integration is mentioned anywhere in Keycard Shell's official documentation, blog, or open-source firmware repo.
Shell provides clear signing that decodes ERC-20 approvals so users retain full visibility and control over ERC20/ERC712 signatures such as approvals before confirming.

As an air-gapped QR/USB signer that returns signed transactions to companion software (e.g. Sparrow, Specter, Rabby), broadcasting is done by the paired wallet which can be pointed at a self-hosted node.
Shell is a stateless offline signing device with no built-in cross-chain bridging functionality described in its docs or repo.
Shell has no persistent state and no portfolio/companion app, so it offers no unified cross-chain account value view; it only signs transactions relayed by third-party wallets.
The keycard-shell GitHub releases page publishes versioned release notes (v1.0.3 through v1.3.0) each with a documented Changes section.

Firmware is cryptographically signed with a key whose public key (bootloader-pubkey.txt) the bootloader uses to verify the firmware before execution, and release commits carry verified GPG signatures.
The README documents a reproducible-build verification flow using tools/firmware-hash.py to hash a locally built binary and match it against the official release binary ('The two hashes must match').
The Keystone Nexus companion app's App Store privacy label discloses collecting Diagnostics Performance Data used for 'Analytics' purposes.
The Keystone Nexus App Store privacy label discloses collecting Diagnostics 'Crash Data' for analytics and app functionality.
No Keystone documentation or app materials mention stealth-address receiving support.
No Keystone documentation or app materials mention Privacy Pools integration.
Keystone signs standard transparent BTC/EVM transactions with no private transfer mode, so transfers are public by default.
Keystone displays approve parameters when signing but its Nexus companion has no built-in allowance manager, relying on third-party tools like Revoke.cash to inspect/revoke.
The Keystone Nexus companion app offers asset swaps but no native cross-chain bridging feature is documented in its FAQ.
Keystone Nexus provides multi-chain asset viewing with a unified/aggregated balance across supported chains.
Keystone supports ENS name resolution/display by loading an offline ENS database, showing the .eth name alongside the on-chain address when signing.
Keystone publishes a public changelog for its companion app with version release notes.
Keystone documents reproducible firmware builds via Docker, letting users compile from source and compare SHA256 checksums against released firmware.
The Keystone 3 firmware repository LICENSE file is the MIT License.
Ledger Live collects anonymous usage/product analytics by default with a toggle under Settings > Help > Analytics, so it does send usage telemetry.
Ledger Live sends crash/error diagnostic reports (a separate 'Report bugs' toggle exists in Settings > Help alongside Analytics), so crash reports are sent by default.
No official Ledger documentation indicates support for stealth-address receiving in Ledger Live or the devices.
There is no evidence in Ledger's official materials of any Privacy Pools integration in Ledger Live or its devices.
Ledger Live sends standard on-chain transfers with no privacy mode, so transfers are public by default.
Ledger Live integrates Revoke.cash to let users inspect and revoke token approvals without leaving the app.
Ledger's open-source SatStack lets Ledger Live connect to a user's own Bitcoin full node to broadcast transactions.
Ledger Live offers native cross-chain bridging/swaps via the integrated LI.FI aggregator.
The Ledger Wallet/Live Home tab aggregates total balance across every account and network into a single unified value view.
Ledger Live resolves ENS names in the send flow, with the mapping cryptographically verified on the hardware device.
Ledger publishes a public CHANGELOG.md and GitHub Releases for Ledger Live, plus a 'What's new' support page.
Ledger firmware/OS and apps are cryptographically signed and verified by the device's genuine check before install.
Ledger's Secure Element firmware is closed-source under STMicroelectronics NDA and is not published as reproducible builds.
Apple App Store privacy disclosure for NGRAVE LIQUID lists 'Product Interaction' and 'Usage Data' collected and used for Analytics.
The App Store privacy section lists Diagnostics including 'Crash Data' and 'Performance Data' collected and used for Analytics.
NGRAVE ZERO/LIQUID supports only standard coins/EVM tokens with QR-signed transactions and offers no stealth-address receiving feature.
No NGRAVE documentation or roadmap mentions any Privacy Pools integration.
Transfers are ordinary on-chain transactions signed offline and broadcast publicly, with no private-transfer mode described.
LIQUID provides no token-approval inspect/revoke feature; NGRAVE's own guidance directs users to external tools like revoke.cash.
The air-gapped ZERO relies on the LIQUID companion app to fetch data and broadcast transactions, with no option to connect a self-hosted node.
NGRAVE offers third-party Changelly swaps and MetaMask/Rabby integration but native in-app bridging is listed as still in development, not available.
LIQUID provides a real-time portfolio overview showing total account value across all supported coins and tokens.
NGRAVE's roadmap lists 'Use ENS names in LIQUID' under Already Available features.
NGRAVE publishes versioned release notes/'What's New' for the LIQUID app on the app stores (e.g. v2.11.1 fixes).
NGRAVE states firmware updates are cryptographically checked and only installed if signed by NGRAVE.
The ZERO firmware is proprietary/closed-source (WalletScrutiny/Walletbeat rate it non-FOSS with an empty public repo), so builds are not independently reproducible.

OneKey's privacy policy states it collects analytics data and uses third parties to analyze traffic, and a Privacy Guides community analysis documents mandatory, non-optional telemetry (device fingerprint/instanceId, IP, geolocation) fired on every app launch.
No OneKey documentation or product page indicates support for stealth-address receiving.
No OneKey documentation or product page indicates any Privacy Pools integration.
OneKey is a standard multi-chain wallet whose send flow broadcasts ordinary on-chain transactions with no private-transfer mode, so transfers are public by default.
OneKey provides ABI parsing and approval prompts at signing time but its own guidance directs users to third-party tools like Revoke.cash rather than an in-app approval inspection/revoke manager.
OneKey App supports adding a custom RPC per network that replaces OneKey's default node, allowing broadcast via a self-hosted node.
OneKey App unifies Swap and Bridge into one aggregator supporting cross-chain transfers across 20+ blockchains.

The OneKey asset panel shows the value of assets under the currently selected wallet account/chain and requires switching chain and account to navigate, rather than presenting a single unified cross-chain account total.
OneKey publishes a public firmware changelog for OneKey Pro with dated version release notes for system and Bluetooth firmware.
OneKey firmware artifacts are built via GitHub CI and signed by the OneKey team before release, with documented verification of the signature.
Trezor Suite collects usage/functional analytics (logged to an AWS S3 backend) when data collection is enabled, a setting prompted on first run and toggleable in Settings.
Trezor Suite sends error/crash reports to Sentry.io to track errors and app performance for users who have anonymous data collection enabled.
No Trezor Suite or firmware documentation references stealth-address receiving; the feature is absent.
There is no Privacy Pools integration in Trezor Suite documentation, changelogs, or the trezor-suite repository.
Trezor Suite sends standard on-chain transactions with no shielded/private transfer mode, so token transfers are public.
Trezor Suite has no general native token-approval inspector/revoker (only a narrow revoke step inside the mobile DEX swap flow) and users are directed to third-party tools for allowance management.
Trezor Suite (desktop) lets users connect to their own full node via a custom Blockbook or Electrum backend, broadcasting through self-hosted infrastructure.
Trezor Suite offers swaps only via third-party CEX/DEX partners (DEX limited to same-chain EVM), with no native cross-chain bridging engine.
The Trezor Suite dashboard shows an aggregate portfolio value combining balances across all enabled coins and accounts with a historical chart.
Trezor publishes public changelogs and release notes for both Suite (GitHub Releases) and firmware.
Official Trezor firmware images are cryptographically signed, requiring at least two independent key-holder signatures.
Trezor firmware builds are reproducible; users can rebuild via Docker and verify the binary is identical to the official image except for the signature bytes.
